title: IAM for beginners: if an access key leaks, what is the maximum damage?
content:
When I first started learning AWS, I usually did everything with a single account that had full permissions. That is convenient until I asked myself: if an access key on my machine or on GitHub leaks, what can whoever finds it do? That question led me to AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).
The first point is telling the types of identities apart. The root user has the highest level of access in the account, and AWS recommends using it only for a few tasks that require it, with MFA enabled. Day-to-day work should use another identity that is granted just enough permissions.
The second point is the type of credentials. Long-term access keys are convenient but risky, because they never expire on their own and can linger in source code, configuration files, or commit history. For people, AWS recommends signing in through IAM Identity Center. For applications running on AWS (EC2, Lambda), use an IAM role to get temporary credentials. The trade-off is that the initial setup is slightly more complex, but in return there is no fixed key to leak.
The third point is the principle of least privilege. Instead of attaching a policy that allows every action on every resource, we allow only the exact actions on the exact resources that are needed. The figure below illustrates this: an IAM user and an IAM role share one policy that allows s3:GetObject but denies s3:DeleteObject on an S3 bucket. According to AWS policy evaluation logic, an explicit deny always wins over an allow, so it can be used to block sensitive actions.
I will verify this with a small lab rather than rely on conclusions from theory:
Create two IAM identities, one with broad permissions and one with narrow permissions. Run the same set of AWS CLI commands with both: list buckets, read an object, delete an object, create an EC2 instance. Record which commands succeed and which are denied (AccessDenied). Use IAM Access Analyzer to see which permissions or access keys were granted but never used. Note: analyzing unused access requires creating a separate unused access analyzer, and it is charged by the number of IAM users and roles analyzed each month, so I check the pricing page first and delete the analyzer when I finish. The result of step 3 shows the real “blast radius” if each identity’s key were leaked.
For operations, I will enable MFA, rotate or delete unused access keys, keep keys out of source code, and regularly review overly broad policies. When the lab ends, temporary users, roles, and keys must be deleted.
My takeaway: least privilege does not prevent a key from leaking, but it limits the consequences when an incident happens. The actual limit depends on the specific policy, so it needs to be tested as above before drawing a conclusion.
References:
Security best practices in IAM: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html IAM roles: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles.html Policy evaluation logic (explicit deny): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html IAM Access Analyzer: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/what-is-access-analyzer.html

title: Overview
content:
AUREL Dining & Wine is a demo restaurant website built with Next.js 15.5.28, React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. The restaurant name, address and dish prices are sample data. This workshop deploys it on AWS: the frontend runs on AWS Amplify Hosting, and the backend is built with AWS SAM (API Gateway HTTP API, Lambda Node.js 22, DynamoDB, Cognito, SES and a private S3 bucket).
Website features
Home, Menu (100 dishes read from the API, filtering, search, pagination), Gallery, About, Contact. Table reservation: a new reservation is a request waiting for confirmation, not a confirmed table. Admin page: sign-in, reservation list with confirm/cancel, menu CRUD, contact messages, image upload to private S3. Source code: https://github.com/ndthuy21/aurel-restaurant
AWS resources may incur charges depending on usage; this setup is not guaranteed to stay within the Free Tier. The examples use the ap-southeast-1 Region.

title: Learning AWS without burning your wallet: easy-to-forget charges when doing labs
content:
When I started doing labs, what worried me most was not a wrong configuration but the bill at the end of the month. My question was: which services can cost money unexpectedly, and how do I spot it early?
The charges that are easy to forget usually come from resources that are “idle but still billed”. An EC2 instance left running is the most obvious example. A NAT Gateway is billed for every hour it exists and for every GB of data that passes through it, partial hours are rounded up to a full hour, and to stop being charged you must delete the NAT Gateway entirely. An EBS volume is still charged for storage while its instance is stopped, and a volume detached from an instance is still charged until it is deleted. A public IPv4 address can also incur hourly charges, even when it is not in use. Exact prices vary by Region and over time, so I always check the official AWS pricing page before drawing conclusions.
To see where the money goes, I use AWS Cost Explorer and group costs by tag. To do that, tags must be applied when the resources are created, for example project=lab, and then activated as cost allocation tags in Billing and Cost Management. According to the AWS documentation, a tag can take up to 24 hours to appear and up to another 24 hours to activate. Cost data for the current period can also be updated with a delay of more than 24 hours, so Cost Explorer is not a real-time alerting tool.
To be warned in advance, I use AWS Budgets. I set a small monthly budget and configure email alerts for when actual or forecasted cost reaches a certain threshold. The trade-off is that, as AWS notes, costs or usage can exceed the threshold before Budgets manages to notify, and Budgets only alerts and does not stop resources by itself.
I will verify this with a small experiment:
Build a lab with a few resources and apply consistent tags. Record the daily cost in Cost Explorer. Compare two scenarios: cleaning up right after the lab versus leaving everything running for a few days. Note the difference and the time from when a charge occurs to when the alert arrives. For operations, I keep a cleanup checklist after every session: stop or delete EC2, delete NAT Gateways, delete unused volumes and snapshots, release Elastic IPs. I also check other Regions, because resources created by mistake in an unfamiliar Region are very easy to forget.
My takeaway: monitoring tools help detect problems early, but the habit of cleaning up is what keeps the bill low. The actual savings can only be concluded once there is data from my own account.
References:
Analyzing your costs and usage with AWS Cost Explorer: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-what-is.html Exploring your data using Cost Explorer (data latency): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/ce-exploring-data.html Managing your costs with AWS Budgets: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/budgets-managing-costs.html Activating user-defined cost allocation tags: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/activating-tags.html Amazon VPC pricing (NAT Gateway, public IPv4): https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/ Why am I charged for Amazon EBS when all my instances are stopped?: https://www.repost.aws/knowledge-center/ebs-charge-stopped-instance

title: Architecture & Data Flow
content:
Data flow (numbers follow the diagram)
The visitor opens the website over HTTPS. AWS Amplify Hosting serves the Next.js static and SSR pages through its CDN. Public requests (GET /menu, POST /reservations, /contact) go from the browser to API Gateway, then to Lambda. The administrator opens the dashboard over HTTPS. The Next.js Admin BFF (/api/auth/* and /api/admin/*) signs in with Cognito and keeps the session in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. The access token is valid for 1 hour. The BFF sends the Bearer access token to API Gateway. /admin/* routes use a JWT authorizer (JWKS validation with Cognito); public routes need no auth. API Gateway applies CORS for the exact origin and throttling. Lambda (Node.js 22, arm64, 256 MB) validates input, rate limits, and queries DynamoDB. Admin routes require an access token and membership of the admin group. The Lambda execution role is limited by ARN to the DynamoDB table, uploads/* in S3 and the SES identity. For media, Lambda returns a signed URL, and the admin uploads (PUT, 120 s) or views (GET, 900 s) the file directly in S3; the file does not pass through Lambda. The bucket is private with Block Public Access and SSE-S3. After a reservation is saved, Lambda calls SES SendEmail (best effort, SES is in the sandbox). There is no queue to retry a failed email. Deployment: the operator pushes code to the source repository and Amplify builds and publishes the frontend automatically. The backend is deployed separately with AWS CLI and SAM through CloudFormation, using a Lambda ZIP stored in a separate S3 artifacts bucket. Data model: one DynamoDB table with keys pk and sk, holding menu, reservations, contacts, slots (seat counters per time slot, maximum 24 guests per slot) and limits (rate limiting with TTL).

title: CloudTrail and GuardDuty: how do you know who did what in an AWS account?
content:
After learning about IAM, I had a follow-up question: if someone uses my key, how do I know what they did and when? That question led me to AWS CloudTrail and Amazon GuardDuty.
CloudTrail records API calls in the account, whether they come from the console, the CLI, or an SDK. Each event shows who made the call, what was called, from which IP address, at what time, and whether it succeeded. By default, the Event history page lets you view management events from the last 90 days in each Region, and viewing is free of charge. To keep a continuous record beyond 90 days, you need to create a trail that delivers logs to S3. AWS recommends using a multi-Region trail so that no activity is missed. The trade-off is that one copy of management events delivered to S3 is not charged by CloudTrail, but I still pay for S3 storage and am responsible for protecting the bucket that holds the logs.
GuardDuty does a different job. It is a threat detection service that continuously analyzes data sources such as CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs, and DNS logs, and then produces findings with a severity from 1.0 to 8.9, where High falls between 7.0 and 8.9. The difference is that CloudTrail gives you raw data to investigate on your own, while GuardDuty proactively alerts you to anything unusual. The two services complement rather than replace each other. The first time GuardDuty is enabled in a Region, the account gets a 30-day trial in that Region; after the trial, usage-based charges apply, so I check the pricing page and set a calendar reminder before the trial ends.
I will verify this with an incident-simulation lab, making use of my digital forensics knowledge:
Create a lab IAM user and use that user’s key to run a few CLI commands, including one that is deliberately denied. Find these events in CloudTrail Event history by user name or event name. Record the time, source IP, and the AccessDenied error code to build a timeline. Generate sample findings in GuardDuty (titles start with [SAMPLE]) to see the structure and severity of an alert. For operations, I would consider a trail that applies to multiple Regions, block public access to the log bucket, and limit who can delete logs. A logging system that an attacker can delete is no longer trustworthy.
My takeaway: CloudTrail answers the question “what happened”, while GuardDuty helps answer “is anything suspicious”. How useful the alerts are has to be verified with a lab in my own account.
References:
Working with CloudTrail event history: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/view-cloudtrail-events.html How CloudTrail works (trail and event history): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/how-cloudtrail-works.html What is Amazon GuardDuty?: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/what-is-guardduty.html Understanding Amazon GuardDuty findings: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty_findings.html Generating sample findings in GuardDuty: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/sample_findings.html Pricing in GuardDuty (30-day free trial): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guardduty/latest/ug/guardduty-pricing.html

title: Step-by-step Lab Guide
content:
Step 1. Run locally (optional check) cd aurel-restaurant pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm setup pnpm dev Open http://127.0.0.1:3000. pnpm setup creates .env.local with a random password and session key. Do not commit this file.
Step 2. Deploy the AWS backend aws configure sso aws sso login --profile YOUR_PROFILE export AWS_PROFILE=YOUR_PROFILE export AWS_REGION=ap-southeast-1 pnpm build:lambda sam validate --lint --template-file infra/template.yaml sam build --template-file infra/template.yaml sam deploy --guided Guided answers for the first deployment:
Stack name: aurel-backend; Region: ap-southeast-1. FrontendOrigin: https://pending.invalid for now (updated in Step 7). SenderEmail: a real email that you own. Open the verification email from AWS and confirm it while the stack is being created. Allow SAM to create IAM roles. Read the stack outputs (ApiUrl, TableName, MediaBucket, UserPoolId, CognitoClientId):
aws cloudformation describe-stacks --stack-name aurel-backend \ --query 'Stacks[0].Outputs' --output table Step 3. Seed the menu export TABLE_NAME=YOUR_TABLE_OUTPUT node dist/seed-aws.mjs The script only adds IDs that do not exist yet and can be run again.
Step 4. Create the admin user in Cognito export USER_POOL_ID=YOUR_POOL_OUTPUT export ADMIN_EMAIL=YOUR_REAL_EMAIL node scripts/create-admin.mjs The password must have at least 14 characters with upper case, lower case, digits and symbols. The script adds the user to the admin group.
Step 5. Prepare SES In the SES sandbox, both the sender and the test recipient must be verified. To send to real guests, request SES production access in the same Region.
Step 6. Deploy the frontend on Amplify Hosting Push the project folder as the root of your GitHub repository (do not push node_modules, .next, .env.local, .data, dist, .aws-sam). In Amplify, choose Create new app, connect the repository and branch, and select Node 22 in the build image. The repository already contains amplify.yml. Add these environment variables before building (never add AWS access keys): Variable Value DATA_MODE aws API_BASE_URL ApiUrl output NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL same ApiUrl, without trailing / COGNITO_CLIENT_ID CognitoClientId output COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID UserPoolId output APP_AWS_REGION ap-southeast-1 APP_ORIGIN exact HTTPS origin of the frontend, without trailing / The default origin looks like https://main.APP_ID.amplifyapp.com. If a build ran before the variables were complete, set them and run the build again.
Step 7. Update the backend CORS origin Run sam deploy --guided again and replace FrontendOrigin with the real Amplify URL. Redeploy the frontend if any variable changed, because NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are packaged at build time.

content: Delete the Amplify app when it is no longer used.
